newsitem.title: USA: Insurance group files suit to stop bank intrusion.
newsitem.headline: Insurance group files suit to stop bank intrusion.

text.p: An insurance industry trade group filed suit this week to block the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency from allowing a bank to sell insurance outside of small towns.

The American Council of Life Insurance said the Comptroller acted improperly in November, 1995, when it allowed Magna Bank of Missouri to retain an insurance business started when the bank operated under Missouri state banking laws.
The bank is owned by holding company Magna Group Inc . Officials there were not immediately available for comment.

"We regret having to take this step," said Gary Hughes, chief counsel of securities and banking for the trade group. "But it had to be taken to prevent banks from entering the business of underwriting insurance through the back door."

The Comptroller's office maintained it acted properly. "We're very confident and comfortable with the analysis we did in the Magna case and feel strongly our decision will be upheld," spokeswoman Janis Smith said.
The lawsuit, filed Jan 7 in U.S. District Court here, charged that the comptroller overstepped its authority, in violation of the National Bank Act.
In 1995, when Magna converted from operating under Missouri banking law to federal law, the comptroller allowed the bank to keep its insurance subsidiary.
Missouri law permitted insurance sales by banks, while federal rules drastically limit such sales.
The comptroller's office determined, however, that federal law allowed a bank converting to a so-called national charter to retain previously operated businesses permitted by state law.
The trade group, which represents 580 life insurance firms, said expanding bank powers was a job for Congress.

"The ACLI remains fully committed to working with the banking industry to develop mutually acceptable legislation to modernize the financial services industry," the group said in a statement. "Financial services reform is a job for Congress and not federal bank regulators."
House banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, who recently introduced a financial services modernization measure, last year sharply criticized the Comptroller's decision in the Magna case.
